questions.question_text: Find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{x^{4}}\,dx$, writing your answer without a negative index.

options.why: Divided by $3$ but lost the negative sign that comes from the new power $-3$.
Added $1$ to the power of the denominator instead of to the index $-4$.
Differentiated $x^{-4}$ instead of finding its primitive.
Divided by the original power $\dfrac{5}{2}$ instead of by the new power $\dfrac{7}{2}$.
Divided by $7$ rather than by the new power $\dfrac{7}{2}$, halving the answer.
Differentiated $x^{\frac{5}{2}}$ instead of finding its primitive.
Raised the power of $11x$ to $2$ but did not divide that term by its new power $2$.
Expanded the brackets but stopped there without finding the primitive.
Integrated each bracket separately and multiplied the results; there is no reverse product rule.

Simplified the fraction but stopped there without finding the primitive.

questions.question_text: Find $\displaystyle\int 5x^{-6}\,dx$, writing your answer without a negative index.

options.why: Divided by $5$ but lost the negative sign that comes from the new power $-5$.
Divided by the new power $-5$ and then cancelled the coefficient $5$ as well, dividing twice.
Differentiated $5x^{-6}$ instead of finding its primitive.
Missed the negative sign that comes from dividing the second term by its new power $-1$.
Multiplied the first term by the new power $\dfrac{4}{3}$ instead of dividing by it.
